title: Pattern and base words

facts.quote: Continuation Pattern A type of chart pattern that occurs in the middle of an existing trend. The previous trend resumes when the pattern is complete.
facts.claim: A continuation pattern forms in the middle of a trend, and the old trend resumes once it completes.

facts.quote: Continuation When price enters and exits a chart pattern in the same direction.
facts.claim: Bulkowski defines a continuation as price entering and leaving a pattern in the same direction.

facts.quote: Reversal Pattern A chart pattern that occurs before an existing trend reverses direction.
facts.claim: A reversal pattern forms before the trend turns the other way.

facts.quote: Reversal When price enters and exits a chart pattern in opposite directions.
facts.claim: Bulkowski defines a reversal as price entering and leaving a pattern in opposite directions.

facts.quote: Just because a pattern forms after a significant advance or decline does not mean it is a reversal pattern.
facts.claim: A pattern that forms after a big move is not automatically a reversal.

facts.quote: Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be classified as either reversal or continuation.
facts.claim: Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be either a reversal or a continuation.

facts.quote: A pattern is not complete or activated until an actual breakout occurs
facts.claim: Fidelity's pattern guide: a pattern is not complete or activated until price actually breaks out.

facts.quote: Confirmation The price at which squiggles on a chart become a valid chart pattern. Usually occurs when price breaks out of the chart pattern trendline boundary.
facts.claim: Confirmation is the price where a shape becomes a valid pattern, usually the breakout through its boundary.

facts.quote: As with the symmetrical triangle, the rectangle pattern is incomplete until a breakout occurs.
facts.claim: A rectangle, like a symmetrical triangle, is incomplete until price breaks out.

facts.quote: A wedge pattern can be either a continuation or a reversal.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a wedge can be either a continuation or a reversal.

facts.quote: Measure rule A method, usually using the chart pattern height, to determine the minimum price move after a breakout
facts.claim: The measure rule uses the pattern's height to estimate a minimum move after the breakout.

facts.quote: Often that's the height added to or subtracted from the breakout price. It is an estimate only.
facts.claim: A pattern's price target is usually its height added to or taken from the breakout price, and it is only an estimate.

facts.quote: The measure rule computation varies from pattern to pattern and is usually inaccurate.
facts.claim: Bulkowski calls the measure rule usually inaccurate.

facts.quote: Any price target should serve as a rough guide, and other factors should also be considered.
facts.claim: StockCharts: any pattern price target is a rough guide.

facts.quote: Stick with original price targets of patterns after conditions have changed
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide lists sticking with a pattern's original target after conditions change among the dangerous habits.

facts.quote: Some of our human tendencies can be dangerous for investors.
facts.claim: The guide introduces that list as human tendencies that can be dangerous for investors.

facts.quote: The Cup with Handle is a bullish continuation pattern that marks a consolidation period followed by a breakout.
facts.claim: The cup with handle is a bullish continuation pattern: a consolidation, then a breakout.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped and resemble a bowl or rounding bottom. A V-shaped bottom would be considered too sharp of a reversal to qualify.
facts.claim: The cup should be a U-shaped bowl; a V-shaped bottom is too sharp to qualify.

facts.quote: After the high forms on the cup's right side, a pullback forms the handle.
facts.claim: The handle is the pullback after the cup's right side makes its high.

facts.quote: The handle represents the final consolidation/pullback before the big breakout and can retrace up to 1/3 of the cup's advance, but usually not more.
facts.claim: The handle is the last pullback before the breakout and usually gives back no more than a third of the cup's advance.

facts.quote: The projected advance after breakout can be estimated by measuring the distance from the right peak of the cup to the bottom of the cup.
facts.claim: The cup's target is its depth, right peak to bottom, projected from the breakout.

facts.quote: A rounded turn that looks like a cup with a handle on the right of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski describes the shape as a rounded turn like a cup, with a handle on the right.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped, but allow variations.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped.

facts.quote: Handle 1 week minimum with no maximum, forming in the upper half of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the handle lasts at least a week and forms in the upper half of the cup.

facts.quote: Cup rims should be near the same price level but be flexible.
facts.claim: The two rims of the cup should sit near the same price.

facts.quote: The handle low (point C ) is a good place to put a stop.
facts.claim: Bulkowski names the handle's low as a good place for the stop.

facts.quote: I looked at 300 cup with handle patterns, stretching from 1990 to March 2024.
facts.claim: Bulkowski studied 300 cup with handle patterns from 1990 to March 2024.

facts.quote: I found that 47% of the cup with handle patterns dropped substantially within two months of the breakout.
facts.claim: In that study, 47% dropped substantially within two months of the breakout.

facts.quote: If a trendline entry is not available, buy when price closes above the right cup rim
facts.claim: Bulkowski's basic entry is a close above the cup's right rim.

facts.quote: Pattern consists of a rounded bottom (not a “V” bottom), two “lips” at each end, and a “handle” (similar to a flag pattern) from the handle
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a rounded bottom, not a V, with a lip at each end and a handle.

facts.quote: Take the height of the right cup lip to the bottom of the cup, then add that amount to the breakout price.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: the cup target is the height from the right lip to the cup's bottom, added to the breakout price.

facts.quote: The buy point occurs when the stock breaks out or moves upward through the old point of resistance (right side of the cup).
facts.claim: Fidelity: the buy point is the breakout through the old resistance at the cup's right side.

facts.quote: The price target following the breakout can be estimated by measuring the distance from the right top of the cup to the bottom of the cup and adding that number to the buy point.
facts.claim: Fidelity: the cup target is the cup's depth added to the buy point.

facts.quote: This should be used only as a guideline.
facts.claim: Fidelity: use the cup's target only as a guideline.

facts.quote: This pattern typically forms over a period of seven to 65 weeks and is characterized by a "U" shaped cup followed by a downward sloping handle.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a U-shaped cup followed by a handle that slopes down.

facts.quote: Avoid handles that are overly deep also, as handles should form in the top half of the cup pattern.
facts.claim: Investopedia: avoid overly deep handles; the handle should form in the top half of the cup.

facts.quote: Place a stop buy order slightly above the upper trend line of the handle.
facts.claim: Investopedia's basic entry is a buy stop just above the handle's upper line.

facts.quote: You can place stop-loss orders below the handle or cup, based on your risk tolerance and market conditions.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the stop can go below the handle or below the cup.

facts.quote: The target with the cup and handle pattern is the height of the cup added to the breakout point of the handle.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the target is the cup's height added to the handle breakout.

facts.quote: A handle defines the proper entry. The highest price in the handle plus 10 cents
facts.claim: IBD: the handle sets the entry, at the handle's highest price plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: A flag is a small rectangle pattern that slopes against the previous trend.
facts.claim: A flag is a small rectangle sloping against the trend before it.

facts.quote: the price action needs to be contained within two parallel trend lines.
facts.claim: A flag's price action sits between two parallel lines.

facts.quote: A pennant is a small symmetrical triangle that begins wide and converges as the pattern matures (like a cone).
facts.claim: A pennant is a small symmetrical triangle whose lines converge.

facts.quote: The flagpole is the distance from the first resistance or support break to the high or low of the flag/pennant.
facts.claim: The flagpole is the sharp move leading into the flag or pennant.

facts.quote: Flags and pennants must be preceded by a sharp advance or decline.
facts.claim: Flags and pennants need a sharp advance or decline before them.

facts.quote: Once a flag is over 12 weeks old, it would be classified as a rectangle.
facts.claim: StockCharts reclassifies a flag older than 12 weeks as a rectangle.

facts.quote: volume expanded on the sharp advance to form the flagpole, contracted during the flag's formation, and expanded right after the resistance breakout.
facts.claim: Volume expands on the pole, contracts in the flag and expands again on the breakout.

facts.quote: The flagpole length can be applied to the resistance break or support break of the flag/pennant to estimate the advance or decline.
facts.claim: A flag or pennant target is the pole's length applied to the breakout.

facts.quote: Flag A continuation chart pattern that generally lasts less than three weeks and resembles a parallelogram that slopes against the prevailing trend.
facts.claim: StockCharts glossary: a flag is a short continuation pattern, a parallelogram sloping against the trend.

facts.quote: Flags appear as small rectangles usually tilted against the prevailing price trend and mounted at the end of a flagpole.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags are small rectangles tilted against the trend, hanging off a flagpole.

facts.quote: If you don't have a straight-line (or a quick move) price run (the flagpole), then you don't have a flag.
facts.claim: No quick, straight-line run (the flagpole), no flag.

facts.quote: Price moves between two parallel, or near parallel, trendlines.
facts.claim: In a flag, price moves between two parallel or near-parallel lines.

facts.quote: Flags are short, less than 3 weeks long. Patterns longer than that are rectangles or channels.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags last under three weeks; longer ones are rectangles or channels.

facts.quote: Prices move between two converging trendlines.
facts.claim: In a pennant, price moves between two converging lines.

facts.quote: Volume trend Downward trend 86% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski found pennant volume trending down 86% of the time.

facts.quote: Pennants are short, 3 weeks long or less. Patterns longer than that are symmetrical triangles
facts.claim: Pennants last three weeks or less; longer ones are symmetrical triangles.

facts.quote: In technical analysis, a flag is a price pattern that moves against the main trend in a shorter time frame, having the appearance of a flag on a flagpole.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a flag moves against the main trend and looks like a flag on a flagpole.

facts.quote: If lines converge, the patterns are referred to as a wedge or pennant pattern.
facts.claim: Investopedia: when the lines converge instead of running parallel, it's a wedge or pennant, not a flag.

facts.quote: In a typical flag pattern, volume will increase during the initial trend and then decrease or hold level during the consolidation period.
facts.claim: Investopedia: volume rises on the initial move and falls or holds level in the flag.

facts.quote: The initial move must be met with large volume, while the pennant should have weakening volume
facts.claim: Investopedia: heavy volume on the pole, weakening volume in the pennant.

facts.quote: The price target is often set by adding the flagpole’s height to the breakout point.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the pennant target adds the flagpole's height to the breakout point.

facts.quote: Pennants have converging trendlines that form a small symmetrical triangle.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a pennant's converging lines form a small symmetrical triangle.

facts.quote: These patterns are often preceded by a steep, sharp price change, up or down, and form a short consolidation that appears like a triangle or flag.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: flags and pennants follow a steep, sharp move and are short consolidations.

facts.quote: Bounded by two trend lines, each headed in the same direction; Price must touch a trend line at least five times (3 times on one and 2 times on the other) before a breakout
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a wedge's two lines point the same way, with at least five touches, three on one line and two on the other.

facts.quote: Performance in both types is below average, and retracements are very common
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: both wedge types perform below average.

facts.quote: Price bounces between two up-sloping and converging trendlines.
facts.claim: A rising wedge sits between two up-sloping lines that converge.

facts.quote: Price should touch (at a minor high or minor low) each trendline at least five times to outline a good pattern. That's 3 touches of one trendline and 2 of the opposite.
facts.claim: Bulkowski wants at least five touches: three on one line and two on the other.

facts.quote: Breakout Can be in any direction but is downward 60% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: rising wedges can break either way; downward 60% of the time.

facts.quote: Rising wedges, especially for downward breakouts, are some of the worst performing chart patterns.
facts.claim: Bulkowski calls rising wedges some of the worst-performing chart patterns.

facts.quote: The pattern confirms as a valid one when price closes outside one of the trendlines.
facts.claim: A wedge confirms only on a close outside one of its lines.

facts.quote: Price follows two down-sloping and converging trendlines.
facts.claim: A falling wedge sits between two down-sloping lines that converge.

facts.quote: The falling wedge is a poor performer as far as bullish chart patterns go.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the falling wedge is a poor performer among bullish patterns.

facts.quote: The Rising Wedge is a bearish pattern that begins wide at the bottom and contracts as prices move higher and the trading range narrows.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the rising wedge is bearish; it narrows as prices rise.

facts.quote: While it is a consolidation formation, the loss of upside momentum on each successive high gives the pattern its bearish bias.
facts.claim: Its bearish bias comes from upside momentum fading on each new high.

facts.quote: In contrast to symmetrical triangles , which have no definitive slope and no bullish or bearish bias, rising wedges definitely slope up and have a bearish bias.
facts.claim: Unlike the neutral symmetrical triangle, the rising wedge slopes up and carries a bearish bias.

facts.quote: The Falling Wedge is a bullish pattern that begins wide at the top and contracts as prices move lower.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the falling wedge is bullish; it narrows as prices fall.

facts.quote: The reaction lows penetrate the previous lows, but this penetration becomes shallower. Shallower lows indicate a decrease in selling pressure
facts.claim: In a falling wedge each new low is only a little lower, which shows selling pressure easing.

facts.quote: Usually, a rising wedge pattern is bearish
facts.claim: Investopedia: a rising wedge is usually bearish.

facts.quote: A falling wedge pattern is seen as a bullish signal
facts.claim: Investopedia: a falling wedge is seen as bullish.

facts.quote: Ascending Triangle A sideways price pattern between two converging trend lines in which the lower line is rising while the upper line is flat.
facts.claim: An ascending triangle has a flat upper line and a rising lower line.

facts.quote: Two trendlines bound prices; the top trendline is horizontal and the bottom one slopes upward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: ascending triangle, flat top line, rising bottom line.

facts.quote: Bounded by a horizontal upper trend line and an upward sloping lower trend line.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: ascending triangle, flat upper line, rising lower line.

facts.quote: It's these higher lows that indicate increased buying pressure and give the ascending triangle its bullish bias .
facts.claim: The rising lows show buyers stepping in higher, which gives the ascending triangle its bullish bias.

facts.quote: Breakout Upward 63% of the time and 64% of the way to the triangle apex (for both breakout directions).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: ascending triangles break upward 63% of the time.

facts.quote: Prices can break in either direction, but more commonly upward
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: an ascending triangle can break either way, more often up.

facts.quote: Descending Triangle A sideways price pattern between two converging trend lines in which the upper trend line is descending while the lower line is flat.
facts.claim: A descending triangle has a flat lower line and a falling upper line.

facts.quote: A price pattern bounded by two trendlines, the bottom one horizontal and the top sloping downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: descending triangle, flat bottom line, falling top line.

facts.quote: Bounded by two trend lines; the lower is horizontal and the upper slopes downward
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: descending triangle, flat lower line, falling upper line.

facts.quote: Breakout Can be in any direction but is upward 53% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: descending triangles break either way; upward 53% of the time.

facts.quote: Prices can break in either direction but most commonly downward
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a descending triangle can break either way, most commonly down.

facts.quote: Regardless of where they form, descending triangles are bearish patterns that indicate distribution.
facts.claim: StockCharts calls descending triangles bearish patterns.

facts.quote: It's because the pattern isn't complete until support is broken.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a descending triangle isn't complete until support breaks.

facts.quote: The pattern confirms as a valid one when price closes outside one of the trendlines.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a descending triangle confirms on a close outside one of its lines.

facts.quote: The symmetrical triangle, which can also be referred to as a coil, usually forms during a trend as a continuation pattern.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the symmetrical triangle is also called a coil.

facts.quote: Symmetrical triangles, sometimes called coils, appear often on the historical price chart but performance is awful.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: symmetrical triangles are sometimes called coils.

facts.quote: A symmetrical triangle pattern, also known as a coil, appears on trading charts when two converging trend lines connect sequential peaks and troughs.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a symmetrical triangle is also known as a coil.

facts.quote: Symmetrical Triangle A sideways chart pattern between two converging trend lines in which the upper trend line is declining and the lower trend line is rising.
facts.claim: A symmetrical triangle has a falling upper line and a rising lower line that converge.

facts.quote: Two trendlines bound prices; the bottom trendline slopes up and the top one slopes down.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: symmetrical triangle, bottom line up, top line down.

facts.quote: Bounded by a downward sloping upper trend line and an upward sloping lower trend line.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: symmetrical triangle, falling upper line, rising lower line.

facts.quote: The ideal breakout point occurs 1/2 to 3/4 of the pattern's development or time span, which can be measured from the apex (convergence of upper and lower lines) back to the beginning of the lower trend line (base).
facts.claim: The apex is where the two lines converge; the ideal breakout comes one-half to three-quarters of the way to it.

facts.quote: A break before the 1/2 way point might be premature, and a break too close to the apex may be insignificant.
facts.claim: A break before halfway may be premature; one too close to the apex may mean little.

facts.quote: Breakout Upward 60% of the time and 74% of the way to the triangle apex (for both breakout directions).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: symmetrical triangles break out about 74% of the way to the apex.

facts.quote: The average distance from the breakout is 61% to 62% of the way to the triangle apex (where the trendlines join).
facts.claim: Bulkowski defines the apex as where the trendlines join.

facts.quote: Price trend Can be any direction leading to the chart pattern.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the trend into a symmetrical triangle can be either direction.

facts.quote: flags and pennants require a sudden shift before they form. Symmetrical triangles can take shape without such a prior movement.
facts.claim: Investopedia: pennants need a sudden prior move; symmetrical triangles don't.

facts.quote: The pattern is usually considered a pennant if it is less than three weeks.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a symmetrical triangle under three weeks is usually called a pennant.

facts.quote: The pattern forms with two consecutive troughs that are roughly equal, a moderate peak in between and a resistance breakout.
facts.claim: A double bottom is two roughly equal troughs with a moderate peak between, then a breakout.

facts.quote: Breaking resistance from the highest point between the troughs completes the Double Bottom Reversal.
facts.claim: A double bottom completes when price breaks above the high between the two lows.

facts.quote: typically, a trough within 3% of its predecessor is considered valid.
facts.claim: StockCharts accepts a second low within 3% of the first.

facts.quote: Two successive troughs separated by a peak
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a double bottom is two troughs separated by a peak.

facts.quote: Price must break out of middle peak
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: price must break out above the middle peak.

facts.quote: This pattern resembles the letter “W” and involves a security or index experiencing two distinct lows at approximately the same level, with rebounds in between.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a double bottom looks like a W, two lows at about the same level.

facts.quote: A long position is recommended on a daily close above the first rebound’s high, with a stop loss at the pattern’s second low.
facts.claim: Investopedia: enter on a daily close above the middle high.

facts.quote: No, there is room to play with the relative levels of the lows, though they should be within 3% to 4% of each other.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the two lows should be within 3% to 4% of each other.

facts.quote: The pattern forms with two prominent peaks that are roughly equal, a moderate trough in-between and a support break.
facts.claim: A double top is two roughly equal peaks, a moderate trough between, then a support break.

facts.quote: Breaking support from the lowest point between the peaks completes the Double Top Reversal.
facts.claim: A double top completes on a break below the low between the peaks.

facts.quote: Perhaps the most important aspect of a Double Top Reversal is to avoid jumping the gun. Wait for support to be broken with an expansion of volume.
facts.claim: Don't jump the gun on a double top; wait for support to break.

facts.quote: Usually, a peak within 3% of the previous high is adequate.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a second peak within 3% of the first is close enough.

facts.quote: Price must break out of middle reversal point
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a double top needs a break of the middle low.

facts.quote: A double top pattern forms when a strong uptrend is followed by two distinct peaks at roughly the same price level with a trough in between.
facts.claim: Schwab: a double top is two peaks at about the same price with a trough between.

facts.quote: There are three equal highs followed by a break below support .
facts.claim: A triple top is three equal highs, then a break below support.

facts.quote: Three distinct peaks at roughly the same price level separated by two intermittent troughs
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a triple top is three peaks at about the same price with two troughs between.

facts.quote: Of these patterns mentioned, only the ascending triangle has bullish overtones; the others are neutral until a break occurs.
facts.claim: Three equal highs can also be part of an ascending triangle, which carries a bullish bias.

facts.quote: Three distinct troughs at roughly the same price level separated by two intermittent peaks at any level
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a triple bottom is three lows at about the same price.

facts.quote: Head and Shoulders Top A bearish reversal pattern marked by three (or more) prominent peaks with a middle peak (the head) that is higher than the other peaks (the shoulders).
facts.claim: A head and shoulders top has a middle peak, the head, higher than the shoulders either side.

facts.quote: The pattern contains three successive peaks, with the middle peak ( head ) being the highest and the two outside peaks ( shoulders ) being low and roughly equal.
facts.claim: Three peaks: the middle one highest, the outer two lower and roughly equal.

facts.quote: The reaction lows of each peak can be connected to form support or a neckline
facts.claim: The neckline connects the lows between the peaks.

facts.quote: The head and shoulders pattern isn't complete, and the uptrend is not reversed until the neckline support is broken.
facts.claim: A head and shoulders isn't complete until the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: This distance is then subtracted from the neckline to reach a price target.
facts.claim: The head-to-neckline distance is subtracted from the neckline for the target.

facts.quote: After breaking neckline support, the projected price decline is found by measuring the distance from the neckline to the top of the head.
facts.claim: The projected decline is the distance from the neckline to the top of the head.

facts.quote: Without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a Head and Shoulders reversal pattern
facts.claim: No prior uptrend, no head and shoulders top.

facts.quote: Neckline In a head-and-shoulders chart pattern, a line joining the armpits, extended into the future to show trading signals when price crosses it.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the neckline joins the armpits, the low points between the peaks.

facts.quote: A three-peak pattern with the middle peak above the others.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: three peaks, the middle one above the others.

facts.quote: Price must have something to reverse, so if the rise leading to the pattern is small, expect a small decline.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a reversal needs something to reverse.

facts.quote: Three peaks with center peak higher than the other two
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: three peaks, the center one highest.

facts.quote: Pattern is only complete on breaking the neckline
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: the pattern is complete only when the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: Target is the distance from the head to the neckline projected from the neckline
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: target is the head-to-neckline distance projected from the neckline.

facts.quote: is formed by drawing a line underneath the troughs established just before and just after the head.
facts.claim: Schwab: the neckline is drawn under the troughs just before and after the head.

facts.quote: Indeed, many investors have paid a steep price for placing a trade without waiting for signals confirming the pattern.
facts.claim: Schwab: many investors have paid for trading the pattern before it confirmed.

facts.quote: Trend reversals require strong trends leading into them.
facts.claim: Schwab: a reversal needs a strong trend leading into it.

facts.quote: In my experience, those new to technical analysis tend to see head-and-shoulders patterns everywhere.
facts.claim: Schwab: newcomers tend to see head and shoulders patterns everywhere.

facts.quote: The pattern contains three successive troughs with the middle trough (head) being the deepest and the two outside troughs (shoulders) being shallower.
facts.claim: A head and shoulders bottom has three troughs, the middle one deepest.

facts.quote: An inverse head and shoulders pattern, often called a head and shoulders bottom, suggests a reversal from a bearish to a bullish trend, formed by three troughs.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the inverse head and shoulders, or head and shoulders bottom, is formed by three troughs.

facts.quote: A 3-valley pattern with the middle valley below the others.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a head and shoulders bottom is three valleys, the middle one lowest.

facts.quote: After the shakeout, the previous trend often reasserts.

facts.claim: Pruden (CMT Association): the cause is built up during a trading range, and the projected move out of it is its effect.

walkthroughs.title: A pause or a turn
steps: Most chart patterns are one of two kinds. A continuation is a pause. Price goes in and comes out the same way.
A reversal is a turn. In one way, out the other. That's where tops and bottoms live.
Either way, it's just a shape until price breaks out of it. The breakout is what makes it a pattern.

walkthroughs.title: The cup and its handle
steps: The cup comes after a run. Price rounds out in a U, like a bowl. A sharp V doesn't count.
The handle is the short pullback off the cup's right side. It should stay in the upper half of the cup.
The buy is price trading through the top of the handle. Mark it the night before and set an alert.
Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day. The handle's low works too.

walkthroughs.title: Lines that frame the pause
steps: A flag needs a pole: a sharp, straight run. Then two parallel lines tilt against it. No pole, no flag.
A pennant is the same idea, but the lines squeeze together like a tiny triangle.
Triangles and wedges have converging lines too. Where the lines meet is the apex.
In a wedge both lines slope the same way. In a triangle they don't.

questions.q: A leader runs hard, then goes sideways for a few weeks. Your buddy calls it a continuation pattern. What's he saying?
choices: A pause, then the trend resumes
A sign the trend is about to flip
Any pattern that breaks out upward
Any sideways range, whatever follows
questions.answer: A pause, then the trend resumes
questions.why: He's calling it a pause. The stock came in going up, and he expects it to leave going up. In one direction, out the same direction, that's the whole test. It works in a downtrend too, where the pause breaks lower. A flag or a base inside a leader's uptrend is exactly this kind of pause. But a sideways range on its own doesn't tell you much yet. The way price leaves the box is what names it.
questions.lesson_line: In one way, out the same way. That's a continuation.

wrong.A sign the trend is about to flip: That's a reversal pattern. The trend turns after it, the opposite of what he's saying.
wrong.Any pattern that breaks out upward: Up isn't the test. A continuation inside a downtrend breaks out lower.
wrong.Any sideways range, whatever follows: Not every range is a pause. A rectangle can turn into a top too. How price leaves decides it.

questions.simple: A pause in the trend. Price goes in one way and comes out the same way.

deeper.example: StockCharts: a continuation forms in the middle of a trend, and the old trend resumes once it completes. Bulkowski's test is direction: price enters and leaves the pattern the same way. StockCharts adds that many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be either kind until price leaves.

questions.q: A stock climbs for months, builds a pattern up top, then leaves it heading down. What kind of pattern was that?
choices: Reversal pattern
Continuation pattern
Flag pattern
Throwback
questions.why: A reversal. It went in rising and came out falling, so the trend turned. Compare the way in with the way out. Opposite directions, you've got a reversal. Same direction, like a flag after a run, you've got a continuation. If you own a stock that leaves a pattern to the downside, your stop is what gets you out.
questions.lesson_line: Reversal: in one way, out the other.

wrong.Continuation pattern: A continuation leaves the same way it came in. This one came in rising and left falling.
wrong.Flag pattern: A flag is a short pause after a sharp run, and the run picks back up after it. This trend turned.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback is price coming back to the breakout level after an upside break. It isn't a pattern.

questions.simple: A reversal. Price went in one way and came out the other way, so the trend turned.

deeper.example: StockCharts: a reversal pattern forms before an existing trend reverses direction. Bulkowski's test is that price enters and leaves the pattern in opposite directions. Flags and pennants are the short continuation kind.

questions.q: A friend says his stock is building a cup with handle. What should you see on the chart?
choices: U-shaped base plus a short pullback
Three peaks, middle one highest
Two equal lows shaped like a W
Lower highs on a flat floor
questions.answer: U-shaped base plus a short pullback
questions.why: A U-shaped base plus a short pullback near the highs. The cup comes after a run. Price sells off, rounds out at the bottom, and climbs back to the old high. Then it rests a little. That rest is the handle. I want the handle tight, with volume drying up. The buy comes as price trades through the top of the handle.
questions.lesson_line: Cup first, handle second, breakout third.

wrong.Three peaks, middle one highest: That's a head and shoulders. A cup is one rounded low.
wrong.Two equal lows shaped like a W: That's a double bottom, two separate lows. A cup is one round U.
wrong.Lower highs on a flat floor: That's a descending triangle, straight lines closing in. A cup is a rounded bowl.

questions.simple: A rounded U-shaped base, then a short dip near the highs. That dip is the handle.

deeper.example: Fidelity: the cup forms after an advance and looks like a bowl or rounding bottom. StockCharts: the cup should be U-shaped, and after the high on its right side, a pullback forms the handle.

questions.q: The cup is done and price is back near the old high. Where on the chart do you look for the handle?
choices: The short pullback after the cup
The deepest low of the whole cup
The run-up before the cup began
The day price breaks out of it
questions.answer: The short pullback after the cup
questions.why: The short pullback after the cup. Once the right side tags its high, price backs off a little. That dip is the handle, the last pause before the breakout. A good one gives back no more than about a third of the cup's climb, and it can drift lower. This is where I want volume to dry up. The top of the handle is your trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The handle is the last pause before the breakout.

wrong.The deepest low of the whole cup: That's the bottom of the cup. The handle forms up near the highs.
wrong.The run-up before the cup began: That's the prior run. A cup needs one, but it isn't the handle.
wrong.The day price breaks out of it: The breakout comes out of the handle. It isn't the handle.

questions.simple: Right after the cup. The handle is the short dip once the right side makes its high.

deeper.example: StockCharts: once the high forms on the cup's right side, a pullback forms the handle. It can retrace up to a third of the cup's advance. Investopedia describes the handle as sloping down.

questions.q: A stock plunges, then rips straight back to the highs in a sharp V. That's the ideal shape for a cup.
questions.why: False. I want a U, not a V. A rounded bottom means the stock spent time down there and the sellers got worked through. That's support getting built. A V turns too fast. Nothing got tested, and it can fall right back. The U doesn't have to be perfect, but it should look like a bowl.
questions.lesson_line: U, not V. The rounded bottom is where support gets built.
questions.simple: False, a cup should be a round U. A sharp V turns too fast to build support.

deeper.example: StockCharts says the cup should be U-shaped like a bowl, and a V-shaped bottom is too sharp a reversal to qualify. Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide say the same, and Bulkowski allows variations, so the U need not be perfect.

questions.q: Everyone in chat says your stock is flagging. What does that look like on the chart?
choices: A brief pause tilting against a run
A long base shaped like a round bowl
Two lines that meet at a point
The sharp run that comes before it
questions.answer: A brief pause tilting against a run
questions.why: A brief pause tilting against a run. The stock rips, and that run is the pole. Then it drifts sideways or a little lower between two parallel lines. That drift is the flag. I like it tight, with volume drying up as it rests. We buy as price trades through the top of the flag. If the lines squeeze to a point, you're looking at a pennant.
questions.lesson_line: A flag leans against the move it interrupts.

wrong.A long base shaped like a round bowl: That's a rounding bottom, or the cup of a cup with handle. A flag is short.
wrong.The sharp run that comes before it: That's the flagpole. The flag is the pause hanging off it.
wrong.Two lines that meet at a point: Lines that meet make a pennant or a triangle. A flag's lines run parallel.

questions.simple: A short pause that leans against the sharp run before it, between two parallel lines.

deeper.example: StockCharts calls a flag a small rectangle that slopes against the previous trend, with price held between two parallel lines. Bulkowski adds that it hangs off a flagpole, a quick run.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short pause can hang off a sharp, near-straight run called the ___.
questions.why: Flagpole. StockCharts: flags and pennants must be preceded by a sharp advance or decline, and the flagpole measures that move. Bulkowski: without a straight-line or quick run, you don't have a flag.
questions.lesson_line: No pole, no flag.
questions.simple: It is the flagpole, the sharp run that the flag hangs off, and with no pole there is no flag.

questions.q: You hear a trader on a stream say 'pennant.' What does he see on the chart?
choices: A tiny triangle after a sharp move
A long, flat-topped base of weeks
A flag-like pause with parallel lines
A deep U-shaped base with a handle
questions.answer: A tiny triangle after a sharp move
questions.why: A tiny triangle after a sharp move. Like a flag, it needs the pole first, a fast run up or down. Then the two lines squeeze together toward a point. Parallel lines would make it a flag. A long, flat-topped base is something else entirely. Both a flag and a pennant are short pauses after a pole. Only the lines differ.
questions.lesson_line: Pennant: a small triangle on a flagpole.

wrong.A long, flat-topped base of weeks: That sounds like an ascending triangle or a flat base. A pennant is short and its lines meet.
wrong.A flag-like pause with parallel lines: Parallel lines make a flag. A pennant's lines come together.
wrong.A deep U-shaped base with a handle: That's a cup with handle, a much longer base.

questions.simple: A tiny triangle right after a sharp move. Its two lines come together.

deeper.example: StockCharts calls a pennant a small symmetrical triangle that begins wide and converges. Like a flag, it must follow a sharp advance or decline. Investopedia also describes converging lines that form a small symmetrical triangle.

questions.q: Two stocks pause after big runs. One's lines run parallel, the other's squeeze together. The first is a flag, the second a pennant.
questions.why: True. Parallel lines, flag. Lines coming together, pennant. Both follow a sharp run and both are short pauses. Some flags only run close to parallel, and that's fine. Don't sweat the geometry. What you're after is a tight rest after a strong move.
questions.lesson_line: Parallel lines: flag. Converging lines: pennant.
questions.simple: True, a flag's lines run side by side while a pennant's lines squeeze toward a point.

deeper.example: StockCharts: a flag sits between two parallel lines, while a pennant is a small triangle whose lines converge. Bulkowski allows a flag's lines to be parallel or near parallel. Investopedia: when the lines converge, it's a wedge or pennant, not a flag.

questions.q: Someone in chat calls a chart a wedge. What makes a wedge a wedge?
choices: Narrowing lines sloping the same way
One flat line and one rising line
Parallel lines tilting against a run
A rounded low with a short dip
questions.answer: Narrowing lines sloping the same way
questions.why: Narrowing lines sloping the same way. Both up is a rising wedge, both down is a falling wedge. That's what sets it apart from a triangle, where one line can be flat or the lines point opposite ways. It's not a flag either, because a flag's lines run parallel. Draw both lines before you name anything.
questions.lesson_line: Wedge: both lines point the same way and squeeze together.

wrong.One flat line and one rising line: That's an ascending triangle. In a wedge neither line is flat.
wrong.Parallel lines tilting against a run: That's a flag. A wedge's lines close in.

questions.simple: Two lines that squeeze together while both slope the same way, both up or both down.

deeper.example: Fidelity's guide: two trend lines, each headed in the same direction. Bulkowski: a rising wedge has two up-sloping, converging lines, a falling wedge two down-sloping ones.

questions.q: A stock keeps stalling at the same high, but every pullback bottoms higher than the last. What are you looking at?
choices: Ascending triangle
Descending triangle
Symmetrical triangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: An ascending triangle. The flat top is a seller parked at one price. The higher lows show buyers stepping in sooner each time. That's the part I like, higher lows pressing into a level. Mark the flat top and set an alert. If you trade it, the break through that top is your trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Flat top, rising lows: ascending triangle.

wrong.Descending triangle: That's the mirror image: a flat bottom with falling highs.
wrong.Symmetrical triangle: In a symmetrical triangle neither line is flat. Here the top is.
wrong.Rising wedge: In a rising wedge both lines slope up. Here the top is flat.

questions.simple: An ascending triangle. The top stays flat while each low comes in higher.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide all draw it with a flat upper line and a rising lower line. StockCharts reads the flat top as supply at one level and the higher lows as buyers stepping in. That gives it a bullish bias.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A flat bottom line with lower and lower highs above it is a ___ triangle.
questions.why: Descending. The lower line is flat and the upper line falls, so the two close in. StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide agree on that shape. The name only says which line slopes. It does not settle the break: Fidelity's guide says most commonly downward, while Bulkowski counts upward breaks 53% of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Flat floor, falling highs: descending triangle.
questions.simple: It is a descending triangle, because the floor stays flat while each rally tops out lower.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: A trader on a stream says a chart is 'coiling.' Which pattern does that word name?
choices: Symmetrical triangle
Head and shoulders top
Rounding bottom
Cup with handle
questions.why: The symmetrical triangle. Its lines slope toward each other, so price gets squeezed into a smaller range, like a spring winding up. Coil just names the shape. It doesn't promise a big move. The pattern shows up a lot, but it tests poorly. So a coil on its own isn't a reason for you to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Coil is another name for the symmetrical triangle.

wrong.Rounding bottom: That's one slow, bowl-shaped low. Nothing narrows to a point.
wrong.Head and shoulders top: Three peaks with the middle one highest. Nothing narrows to a point.
wrong.Cup with handle: A rounded cup with a handle on its right. Nothing narrows to a point.

questions.simple: The symmetrical triangle. Its two lines squeeze price into a smaller and smaller range.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts, Bulkowski and Investopedia all give coil as another name for the symmetrical triangle. Bulkowski says the pattern appears often but its performance is awful.

questions.q: You draw both lines of a triangle and extend them to the right. What's the apex?
choices: Where the two lines meet
The widest part of the pattern
The breakout day's high
The first low in the pattern
questions.why: Where the two lines meet. Extend both lines forward, and the point where they cross is the apex. It's not the breakout. Price tends to leave well before the lines meet. A triangle that drifts all the way into its apex has used up its range, and that break means less.
questions.lesson_line: The apex is where a triangle's lines meet.

wrong.The widest part of the pattern: That's the start of the triangle, the opposite end from the apex.
wrong.The breakout day's high: The breakout is where price leaves the pattern, and that comes before the apex.
wrong.The first low in the pattern: That's just the first touch of the lower line.

questions.simple: The point where the triangle's two lines meet, at its narrow end.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts calls the apex the convergence of the upper and lower lines, and Bulkowski says it is where the trendlines join. Bulkowski measures a breakout as part of the way to the apex, so price leaves before the lines meet.

questions.q: Your buddy says a stock just put in a double bottom. What should the chart show?
choices: Two similar lows with a peak between
Two similar highs with a dip between
Three lows at about the same price
A slow, rounded low over months
questions.answer: Two similar lows with a peak between
questions.why: Two similar lows with a peak between. It looks like a W. Price sells off, bounces, then comes back down to test the first low. That second test holding is the interesting part. The peak in the middle of the W is the level that still has to break before you've got anything.
questions.lesson_line: Double bottom: a W, two lows near the same price.

wrong.Two similar highs with a dip between: Those are highs. That's a double top. A double bottom is built from lows.
wrong.A slow, rounded low over months: That's a rounding bottom, one slow bowl, not two separate lows.
wrong.Three lows at about the same price: That's a triple bottom. A double bottom has two lows.

questions.simple: Two lows near the same price with a peak between them, like a W.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts describes two roughly equal troughs with a moderate peak between them. Investopedia says it looks like the letter W. Fidelity's guide calls it two troughs separated by a peak.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A peak, a dip, then a second peak near the same price make the shape of a ___ top.
questions.why: Double. StockCharts describes two roughly equal peaks with a moderate trough between. Schwab says the same: two peaks at about one price. Triple would need three peaks.
questions.lesson_line: Double top: two peaks near one price, with a dip between.
questions.simple: It is a double top, because two peaks at about the same price with a dip between make that shape.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: After a long run, a stock you own prints three peaks: the middle one highest, the outer two about level. Name it.
choices: Head and shoulders
Triple top
Descending triangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: Head and shoulders. The middle peak is the head, and the two lower peaks beside it are the shoulders. A triple top would have all three at about the same height. If you own it, pay attention. That right shoulder is a lower high, a leader losing steam. Know where your stop is.
questions.lesson_line: Head above, shoulders level on either side.

wrong.Triple top: A triple top has three peaks at about the same price. Here the middle one stands taller.
wrong.Rising wedge: That's two rising lines squeezing together, with no head.
wrong.Descending triangle: A triangle's lines meet at a point. Here the middle peak stands above the other two.

questions.simple: Head and shoulders. The middle peak, the head, stands above the two lower peaks beside it.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide all call the middle peak the head. The two lower, roughly equal peaks on either side are the shoulders.

questions.q: You spot a head and shoulders top on a stock you own. Where do you draw the neckline?
choices: Line through the lows between peaks
Line across the two shoulder tops
The highest point of the head
The uptrend line under the whole move
questions.answer: Line through the lows between peaks
questions.why: Through the lows between the peaks. Connect the dip after the left shoulder and the dip after the head. That line can slope up or down, it doesn't have to be level. It's the floor of the whole pattern. Until price breaks it, the top isn't finished. Mark it, because a break under it means the top is done.
questions.lesson_line: The neckline is the floor of the top. The break of it decides the pattern.

wrong.Line across the two shoulder tops: That line sits up top. The neckline runs through the dips.
wrong.The highest point of the head: That's the head's peak. It's used to measure a target, not to draw the neckline.
wrong.The uptrend line under the whole move: That's a trendline. The neckline runs through the pattern's own lows.

questions.simple: Through the low points between the peaks. A break under that line finishes the top.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts connects the reaction lows of each peak, and Bulkowski says the neckline joins the armpits. Schwab draws it under the troughs just before and after the head. Bulkowski allows an up-sloping or a down-sloping neckline.

questions.q: Someone calls the bottom on your chart an inverse head and shoulders. What should you see?
choices: Three lows, the middle one deepest
Three peaks, middle one highest
Two equal lows, a peak between
Three equal lows in a row
questions.answer: Three lows, the middle one deepest
questions.why: Three lows, the middle one deepest. Flip a head and shoulders top upside down and that's it. The deep middle low is the head. The two higher lows on either side are the shoulders. If all three sat near the same price, you'd call it a triple bottom. For a buyer, the line that matters is the neckline across the rally highs between the lows. Until price trades through it, it's just a shape on your watchlist.
questions.lesson_line: Flip a head and shoulders top and you get the bottom version.

wrong.Three peaks, middle one highest: That's the top version, built from peaks.
wrong.Two equal lows, a peak between: That's a double bottom, two lows, not three.
wrong.Three equal lows in a row: That's a triple bottom. Here the middle low has to be the deepest.

questions.simple: Three lows with the deepest one in the middle. It's a head and shoulders turned upside down.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts describes three troughs with the middle trough deepest. Bulkowski calls it a 3-valley pattern with the middle valley below the others. Investopedia says it is often called a head and shoulders bottom.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A rounding bottom is also called a ___ bottom.
questions.why: Saucer. The StockCharts glossary: a rounding bottom, also known as a saucer bottom, is a reversal pattern built over a long consolidation. Bulkowski calls its rims saucer lips. He looks for a rounded bowl shape, usually over many months.
questions.lesson_line: Rounding bottom and saucer: same slow bowl.
questions.simple: It is a saucer bottom: a long, slow, rounded low shaped like a bowl.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f148)

questions.q: The textbooks call the base on your screen a rectangle. What's price doing?
choices: Sideways between flat top and bottom
A narrowing range that slopes upward
A U-shaped dip and slow recovery
Three peaks, the middle highest
questions.answer: Sideways between flat top and bottom
questions.why: Moving sideways between a flat top and a flat bottom. Same thing as a trading range. The shape alone gives you no direction. A rectangle can be a top or a pause, and it isn't done until price breaks out one side. Mark both lines. The break picks the direction, not you.
questions.lesson_line: Rectangle: flat ceiling, flat floor, price bouncing between.

wrong.A narrowing range that slopes upward: That's a rising wedge. A rectangle's lines stay flat and never meet.
wrong.A U-shaped dip and slow recovery: That's a cup. A rectangle is a box.

questions.simple: Moving sideways between a flat top and a flat bottom, like a trading range.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10)

deeper.example: StockCharts says rectangles are also called trading ranges, consolidation zones or congestion areas. They can be a reversal or a continuation, and are incomplete until a breakout. Bulkowski describes flat tops and flat bottoms between two parallel lines.

questions.q: A pattern on your chart looks finished, but price hasn't broken out of it yet. The pattern is confirmed.
questions.why: False. A shape is just a shape until price breaks out of it. No breakout, no pattern. Plenty of perfect-looking bases roll over before they ever trigger. That's why we buy as price trades through the trigger, not before. Until then it's a name on your watchlist.
questions.lesson_line: No breakout, no pattern. The shape alone confirms nothing.
questions.simple: False, a pattern only counts once price breaks out of it. A finished look isn't enough.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: Fidelity's guide says a pattern is not complete or activated until an actual breakout occurs. Bulkowski defines confirmation as the price where squiggles become a valid pattern, usually a break through its boundary. StockCharts says a rectangle is incomplete until a breakout.

questions.story: A stock runs from $40 to $60 in two months. It then moves sideways in a tight range for three weeks. Next it breaks out above the range.
questions.q: Looking back now, what was that three-week range?
choices: Continuation pattern
Trend reversal pattern
Too soon to name it
Throwback
questions.why: A continuation pattern. It came in rising, $40 to $60, and it left rising, out the top of the range. In one way, out the same way. That's the pause we want to find in a leader: a big run, then a tight rest. The break above the range is the trigger. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a pattern by how price enters and leaves it.

wrong.Trend reversal pattern: A reversal leaves the opposite way it came in. This came in rising and left rising.
wrong.Too soon to name it: It already broke out the top. In rising, out rising, so you can name it.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback comes after an upside break, a dip back to the breakout price. This range came before the break.

questions.simple: A continuation. Price came into the range going up and left it going up.

deeper.counter: Keep the same three-week range, but picture a long slide into it before the breakout above. Now price entered falling and left rising, and Bulkowski calls that a reversal. The box looks the same in both cases. The direction in and the direction out decide the name.
deeper.example: Bulkowski defines a continuation as price entering and leaving a pattern in the same direction. StockCharts says a continuation forms in the middle of a trend, and the old trend resumes when it completes.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Your stock had a huge run and is now basing. Because the base formed after a big advance, it's a reversal.
questions.why: False. Where a pattern forms doesn't decide it. How price leaves does. Plenty of leaders base after a huge run and then go right on higher. Out the top, the base was a pause. Out the bottom, it was a top. So don't sell a strong stock just because it ran. Let the break tell you, and let your stop handle the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Where a pattern forms doesn't decide its type. How price leaves it does.
questions.simple: False, a base after a big run can be just a pause. How price leaves it decides the type.

reasons: fixed before (statement reworded by the checker)

deeper.example: StockCharts: a pattern that forms after a big advance or decline is not automatically a reversal. Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be either kind, and Investopedia says a wedge can be too. Bulkowski's test is how price leaves: the same way it came in is a continuation.

questions.q: Cup low $40. Right lip and breakout $50. Add the cup's depth to the breakout. Where's the textbook target?
questions.why: $60. The cup is $50 minus $40, so it's $10 deep. Add that $10 to the $50 breakout and you get $60. That's the textbook way to measure it, and it's a rough guide only. Price can stall well short of it or run right past it. We sell into strength as the stock pushes, not at a printed number.
questions.lesson_line: Cup target: the cup's depth added to the breakout. A guide, not a promise.
questions.simple: $60, because the cup is $10 deep and $50 plus $10 is $60. Treat it as a rough guide.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$10: That's just the cup's depth. You still have to add it to the $50 breakout.
wrong.$50: That's the breakout itself. Add the $10 depth to it.
wrong.$90: You added the $40 low to the breakout. Add the depth, $50 minus $40, instead.

deeper.example: StockCharts, Fidelity and Investopedia all measure a cup's target this way. Fidelity says to use it only as a guideline.

questions.story: A stock builds a cup from $50 down to $35 and back up to $49. Then it pulls back to $38 over two weeks.
questions.q: Would you buy the break out of that pullback as a handle?
choices: No, it sank into the lower half
Yes, any dip after a cup works
Yes, a deep handle shakes out
No, a handle can only go flat
questions.answer: No, it sank into the lower half
questions.why: No. The cup climbs from $35 to $49, and the pullback sinks to $38. That's way down near the $35 low, deep in the lower half of the cup. It isn't a handle, it's the stock giving back most of the cup. A handle should stay up near the highs and stay tight. Drifting a little lower is fine. Diving this deep is a broken base.
questions.lesson_line: A handle that sinks into the bottom of the cup isn't a handle.

wrong.Yes, any dip after a cup works: Where the dip ends matters. A handle stays in the cup's upper half.
wrong.Yes, a deep handle shakes out: Depth isn't a plus here. The overly deep handles are the ones to avoid.
wrong.No, a handle can only go flat: Right answer, wrong reason. A handle can drift lower. The problem is how deep this one went.

questions.simple: No, the dip fell to $38, deep in the lower half of the cup. A handle stays up high.

deeper.trap: Any dip after a cup looks like a handle, so it's tempting to buy its break. Check where the dip ended first. Here the cup climbs from $35 to $49, and the dip gives back most of that by reaching $38. StockCharts says a handle can retrace up to a third of the cup's advance, but not more.
deeper.example: Bulkowski says the handle forms in the upper half of the cup, and Investopedia says to avoid overly deep handles. Investopedia's own description has the handle sloping down, so slope is not the fault.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10); Investopedia unreachable for this check, Bulkowski confirmed

questions.q: Your cup with handle is set up and you want in. Where does the buy go?
choices: Just above the handle's high
At the lowest point of the cup
Halfway down the handle
At the first up day in the cup
questions.why: Just above the handle's high. That's the trigger. We buy as price trades through it during the day, not on a guess inside the pattern. Mark the level the night before and set an alert, so you buy the break instead of chasing it later. Then your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the break out of the handle, not a guess inside the pattern.

wrong.At the lowest point of the cup: That's buying a falling stock before any pattern exists.
wrong.Halfway down the handle: That's a guess inside the pattern, before it breaks out.
wrong.At the first up day in the cup: Way too early. The cup isn't finished and there's no handle yet.

questions.simple: Just above the handle's high, as price breaks out of the pattern.

deeper.example: IBD puts the entry at the handle's highest price plus 10 cents. Investopedia places a buy stop slightly above the handle's upper trend line. Fidelity uses the break through the cup's right side, and Bulkowski a close above the right cup rim.

questions.q: You're marking up a cup with handle the night before. What's a lip?
choices: A high at the cup's top edge
The lowest point of the cup
The lowest price in the handle
The breakout day's close
questions.answer: A high at the cup's top edge
questions.why: A high at the cup's top edge. There are two: one where the cup starts, and one where the right side tops out. You want them near the same price, with some give. The right lip is the one I watch. It's the old high the stock has to work back to, and the handle forms just under it. Mark both lips the night before so the base is clear when you open the chart.
questions.lesson_line: Two lips, one each side of the cup, near the same price.

wrong.The breakout day's close: That's the breakout. The lips come before it.
wrong.The lowest price in the handle: That's the handle's low. The lips are the cup's two top edges.

questions.simple: A high at the top edge of the cup. There's one on each side, near the same price.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f195)

deeper.example: Fidelity's guide describes two lips, one at each end of the cup. Bulkowski measures his target from the right cup lip and wants the two rims near the same price, with some give.

questions.q: The flagpole ran from $20 to $30. The flag breaks out at $28. Add the pole to the breakout. Where's the target?
questions.why: $38. The pole is $30 minus $20, so $10 long. Add that $10 to the $28 breakout and you get $38. That's the measured move. It's an estimate, not an order. If the stock is ripping into it, you sell some into the push. If it stalls early, you don't wait around for $38.
questions.lesson_line: Flag target: the pole's length added to the breakout.
questions.simple: $38, because the pole is $10 long and $28 plus $10 is $38. It's only an estimate.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$40: You added the length to the $30 pole top. Add it to the $28 breakout.
wrong.$58: You added the $30 pole top to the breakout. Add the pole's length, $10.
wrong.$10: That's the pole's length alone. Add it to the breakout.

deeper.example: StockCharts applies the flagpole length to the breakout to estimate the move, and Investopedia sets the pennant target the same way. Bulkowski says a target is an estimate only.

questions.story: A stock jumps 25% in six sessions on heavy volume. Then it drifts lower for eight days between two parallel lines, and volume dries up.
questions.q: What's that eight-day drift?
choices: Flag
Pennant
Rectangle
Double top
questions.why: A flag. The 25% jump on heavy volume is the pole. Eight days drifting lower between parallel lines is the flag. Volume drying up while it rests raises the grade. Now mark the top of the flag, because that's your trigger. We buy as price trades through it, with the stop a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Pole, then a short parallel drift as volume dries up: that's a flag.

wrong.Pennant: A pennant's lines come together. These run parallel.
wrong.Double top: That needs two peaks near the same price. This is one run and a drift.
wrong.Rectangle: A rectangle is flat and longer. Here you've got a short drift that leans against the run.

questions.simple: A flag. A short drift between two parallel lines on light volume, right after a sharp run.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts calls a flag a small rectangle that slopes against the previous trend, with volume contracting as it forms. Bulkowski says flags are short, less than 3 weeks long, so eight days fits.

questions.q: Your stock's flag has been drifting for four months now. It's still a flag.
questions.why: False. Four months isn't a flag anymore. A flag is a short rest right after a sharp run, days to a few weeks. Drift for months and the pole is old news. By then it's a rectangle or a channel, a base. Call it what it's become and judge it as a base.
questions.lesson_line: A long flag stops being a flag. Call it what it has become.
questions.simple: False, flags are short pauses. One that drifts for four months has turned into a base.

deeper.trap: The sources don't agree on where a flag ends. Bulkowski cuts it at under three weeks. StockCharts allows up to 12 weeks before it calls the pattern a rectangle. A two-month drift is a flag to one and a rectangle to the other. That's why this question uses four months, past both limits.
deeper.example: Bulkowski says flags last less than three weeks, and longer patterns are rectangles or channels.

reasons: fixed before (checker changed months to four months)

questions.q: Volume usually dries up while a pennant forms.
questions.why: True. You want a loud pole and a quiet pennant. Heavy volume drives the run, then volume dries up while it rests. In one big study, volume trended down in 86% of pennants. So not every one. It's a plus that raises the grade, and a pennant without it can still work.
questions.lesson_line: Loud pole, quiet pennant. Volume drying up raises the grade.
questions.simple: True. Volume is heavy on the run and then dries up while the pennant forms.

reasons: rests on a study count (Bulkowski's 86%) that he updates over time

deeper.example: Investopedia says the initial move must be met with large volume, while the pennant should have weakening volume. Bulkowski found pennant volume trending down 86% of the time. In StockCharts' flag example, volume expands again right after the breakout.

questions.q: You're drawing a rising wedge. At least how many touches across both lines do Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide want?
questions.why: Five. 3 touches on one line plus 2 on the other makes 5. Any two points make a line, so two touches prove nothing. The extra touches show price really respects both lines. With fewer, you're drawing lines through noise, and I wouldn't call it a wedge yet.
questions.lesson_line: Count the touches: three on one line, two on the other.
questions.simple: Five. Three touches on one line and two on the other.

reasons: computed key

choices: 3 touches
4 touches
5 touches
6 touches

wrong.3 touches: You counted one line only. The other line needs touches too.
wrong.4 touches: Two on each line isn't enough. One line needs three.
wrong.6 touches: Three on each line is more than they ask for.

deeper.example: On a rising wedge, Bulkowski wants at least five touches: 3 on one trendline and 2 on the other. Fidelity's guide asks the same of a wedge before a breakout.

questions.q: Your stock grinds higher in a rising wedge, and each push is weaker than the last. Which way do textbooks lean?
choices: Bearish, though prices are rising
Bullish, as prices are rising
Neutral until it hits the apex
Bullish, like a falling wedge
questions.why: Bearish, even though price is rising. Each new high comes with less push behind it. The squeeze shows buyers running out of gas. If you own a leader that starts doing this, that's your cue to watch your trail closely. The falling wedge is the one with the bullish lean.
questions.lesson_line: Rising wedge: higher prices, weaker pushes. Textbooks lean bearish.

wrong.Bullish, as prices are rising: Rising prices are the trap. The squeeze shows the upside running out of steam.
wrong.Neutral until it hits the apex: No lean is the symmetrical triangle. The rising wedge leans bearish.
wrong.Bullish, like a falling wedge: That mixes up the two. The falling wedge leans bullish, the rising one bearish.

questions.simple: Bearish. Each push higher has less force behind it, even though price is going up.

reasons: fixed before (checker edited a wrong-note)

deeper.example: StockCharts calls the rising wedge bearish: the loss of upside momentum on each new high gives it that bias. Investopedia says it is usually bearish.

questions.q: Rising wedges don't only break down. Plenty of them break up.
questions.why: True. They lean bearish, but in one big study only about 60% broke down. That leaves a lot breaking up. A lean isn't a forecast, so don't act on the shape. Wait for price to actually break one of the lines and show you. If you own one, a break of the lower line is your cue to be out.
questions.lesson_line: A lean is not a forecast. Wait for the break.
questions.simple: True, a rising wedge breaks down more often than not, but plenty still break up.

deeper.trap: Because most rising wedges break down, it's tempting to act before the break. Bulkowski counts downward breaks 60% of the time, so many still break up. He counts a wedge as valid only once price closes outside a trendline. Acting early is a bet on the shape, not on the break.
deeper.example: Bulkowski says a rising wedge can break in any direction, but goes down 60% of the time. Investopedia calls it usually bearish, not always.

reasons: rests on a study count (Bulkowski's 60%) that he updates over time

questions.story: A stock slides for four months. Its lower highs and lower lows trace two down-sloping lines that converge. Each new low is only a bit lower.
questions.q: Which pattern is this?
choices: Falling wedge
Descending triangle
Bear flag
Symmetrical triangle
questions.why: A falling wedge. Both lines slope down and close in, and each new low is only a little lower. That tells you the selling is losing force. Textbooks read it as bullish. But it only counts once price breaks out the top. Until then it's still a downtrend, and I'm not buying a downtrend. And if it's under the 200-day, it's a hard no for a stock anyway.
questions.lesson_line: Both lines falling and closing in: falling wedge. Textbooks lean bullish.

wrong.Descending triangle: That needs a flat bottom line. Here the lows keep falling.
wrong.Bear flag: A bear flag tilts up against the fall, between parallel lines. These lines slope down and close in.
wrong.Symmetrical triangle: Its lower line rises. Here both lines slope down.

questions.simple: A falling wedge. Both lines slope down and close in, and each low is only a bit lower.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: Bulkowski describes both lines sloping down and converging. StockCharts says the shallower new lows show selling pressure easing. StockCharts and Investopedia both read the falling wedge as bullish.

questions.story: Over three months a stock makes lower highs and higher lows. The upper line slopes down, the lower line slopes up, and they're closing in.
questions.q: What's forming here?
choices: Symmetrical triangle
Ascending triangle
Rectangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: A symmetrical triangle. Lower highs and higher lows, so the lines slope toward each other. Neither line is flat, which rules out an ascending or descending triangle. They don't point the same way either, so it's not a wedge. This one has no lean. The break sets the direction, so you wait for it.
questions.lesson_line: Lower highs plus higher lows, closing in: symmetrical triangle.

wrong.Ascending triangle: That needs a flat top line. Here the highs keep falling.
wrong.Rectangle: A rectangle's lines are flat and parallel. They never meet.
wrong.Rising wedge: In a wedge both lines slope the same way. Here they point opposite ways.

questions.simple: A symmetrical triangle. One line falls, the other rises, and neither line is flat.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide describe a falling upper line and a rising lower line that converge. StockCharts gives this triangle no bullish or bearish bias, so the break sets the direction.

questions.q: Your symmetrical triangle keeps getting narrower. When does the textbook want price to break out?
choices: Half to three-quarters of the way in
Right at the apex of the triangle
In the first few days of the pattern
Only after price passes the apex
questions.answer: Half to three-quarters of the way in
questions.why: Half to three-quarters of the way in. Measure from where the lines start to the apex. A break before halfway can be early and fail. A break right at the apex means little, because the range is used up. In one big study the breaks came about 74% of the way in, right in that zone. I don't trade off this ratio. It just tells you a triangle that drifts into its point has run out of room.
questions.lesson_line: Good triangle breaks come before the apex, not at it.

wrong.In the first few days of the pattern: Too early. A break before halfway can be premature.
wrong.Only after price passes the apex: Past the apex the lines have met. There's no pattern left to break.
wrong.Right at the apex of the triangle: A break that close to the apex means little. The range is used up.

questions.simple: Halfway to three quarters of the way to the apex. Breaks too early or too late mean less.

deeper.example: StockCharts puts the ideal breakout at 1/2 to 3/4 of the pattern's time span. Measure from the start of the lower line to the apex. Bulkowski's table puts the breakout 74% of the way to the apex.

reasons: cites a study figure (Bulkowski's 74%) that he updates over time

questions.q: Your stock just put in a second low near the first one and is bouncing. When is the double bottom done?
choices: When price clears the middle peak
When the second low holds a day
When the second low matches the first
When volume spikes at the second low
questions.answer: When price clears the middle peak
questions.why: When price clears the middle peak. That's the top of the middle of the W. Matching lows and a bounce make it possible, but nothing's finished yet. The middle peak is your trigger. If you're buying it, that's the level, and your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: A W isn't done until price clears the middle of the W.

wrong.When the second low holds a day: Holding is a start. The middle peak still has to break.
wrong.When the second low matches the first: Matching lows make it possible. They don't finish it.
wrong.When volume spikes at the second low: Volume at the low doesn't finish it. Only the break above the middle peak does.

questions.simple: Only when price breaks above the peak between the two lows.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts says breaking resistance from the highest point between the troughs completes it. Fidelity's guide says price must break out of the middle peak. Investopedia waits for a daily close above the first rebound's high.

questions.q: First low $50.00, second low $49.00. How far under the first low did the second one go?
questions.why: 2%. $50.00 minus $49.00 is a $1 gap. Divide $1 by $50.00 and you get 2%. That's close enough to call the lows roughly equal, since the textbooks allow about 3%. A small undercut of the first low isn't a problem. Equal-ish lows are one piece of the W. The break over the middle peak still finishes it.
questions.lesson_line: Two lows within about 3% of each other still count as roughly equal.
questions.simple: 2%, a $1 gap on a $50.00 low. That's close enough to call the lows about equal.

reasons: computed key
fixed before (checker edited the lesson line)

wrong.98%: That's the second low as a share of the first, not the gap.
wrong.50%: You flipped it. Divide the gap by the first low, not the other way.

deeper.example: StockCharts accepts a second low within 3% of the first. Investopedia says the lows should be within 3% to 4% of each other.

questions.story: A stock peaks at $80, dips to $70, then rallies to $79.50 and turns down. It now sits at $72.
questions.q: Is this a finished double top?
choices: Not yet, it must break below $70
Yes, the second peak failed
Yes, two peaks at about one price
No, the peaks must match exactly
questions.answer: Not yet, it must break below $70
questions.why: Not yet. A double top is done when price breaks the low between the peaks. Here that's $70, and the stock is still at $72. The peaks don't have to match: $79.50 against $80 is close enough. Don't jump the gun. Until $70 breaks, you're looking at a pullback inside a range.
questions.lesson_line: Don't jump the gun on a double top. Wait for the middle low to break.

wrong.Yes, the second peak failed: A failed second peak sets it up. It doesn't finish it.
wrong.Yes, two peaks at about one price: Two peaks make it possible. The break of $70 finishes it.
wrong.No, the peaks must match exactly: Exact peaks aren't needed. The textbooks call a second peak within 3% of the first close enough.

questions.simple: Not yet. It's only done when price breaks below $70, the low between the peaks.

deeper.trap: Two peaks at almost the same price feel like a finished top, and the turn down from $79.50 feels like proof. It isn't. Until $70 breaks, the slide is only a pullback inside a range. StockCharts calls avoiding jumping the gun perhaps the most important part of a double top.
deeper.example: StockCharts says breaking support from the lowest point between the peaks completes a double top. It calls a second peak within 3% of the first adequate. Fidelity's guide wants a break of the middle low.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.story: After a long climb, a stock makes three peaks: $48, $55, then $48.50. The dips between them both bottomed near $44. Price now sits at $45.
questions.q: What finishes this head and shoulders top?
choices: A close under the $44 neckline
A new high above the $55 head
Another peak near the $48 shoulder
Nothing, three peaks complete it
