questions.why: A close under the $44 neckline. The neckline runs through the two dips between the peaks, both near $44. At $45 the pattern isn't done, it's a warning. If you're still long here, your stop should already be set. A break under $44 means the top is finished and the uptrend is over.
questions.lesson_line: The neckline break is the signal. The shape alone is a warning.

wrong.Nothing, three peaks complete it: Three peaks are only a warning. The top isn't done until $44 breaks.
wrong.A new high above the $55 head: That would put price above the head. A top finishes on a break lower.
wrong.Another peak near the $48 shoulder: Both shoulders are already in. The missing piece is the neckline break.

questions.simple: A close under the $44 neckline, the line through the dips between the peaks.

reasons: fixed before (checker swapped f145 for f196)

deeper.example: StockCharts: the pattern isn't complete, and the uptrend isn't reversed, until neckline support breaks. Bulkowski confirms it on a close below the neckline.

questions.q: Head at $60, neckline at $50. Measure head to neckline and take that off the neckline. What's the target?
questions.why: $40. The head sits $60 minus $50, so $10 above the neckline. Take that $10 off the $50 neckline and you land at $40. It only applies once the neckline breaks, and it's a rough guide at best. On the long side, the useful part is the warning. A leader that breaks its neckline is one you want to be out of.
questions.lesson_line: Head-to-neckline height, projected down from the neckline. A guide, not a promise.
questions.simple: $40, because the head sits $10 above the $50 neckline, and $50 minus $10 is $40.

deeper.trap: A measured target feels precise because it's arithmetic. Bulkowski calls the measure rule usually inaccurate, and StockCharts says any target is a rough guide. Use the $40 as a rough marker, not as a promise of where price will go.
deeper.example: StockCharts subtracts the head-to-neckline distance from the neckline, and Fidelity's guide projects it down from the neckline too.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$10: That's just the head's height over the neckline. Take it off the $50 neckline.
wrong.$30: You took the $10 off the neckline twice.
wrong.$20: You doubled the $10 and stopped there.

questions.story: A stock builds a flat floor at $30 with lower highs above it. Textbooks call the pattern bearish. You have no position.
questions.q: You don't own it. What's your move?
choices: Wait for price to break a line
Short now, the pattern is bearish
Buy now, the floor will hold
Wait for a bounce off $30, then buy
questions.answer: Wait for price to break a line
questions.why: Wait for price to break a line. Textbooks call this triangle bearish, but in one big study 53% broke up. So the label isn't an edge. Shorting on the label is a bet the numbers don't back. Buying a bounce off $30 is a guess too. If it breaks up through the falling top line, that's a trigger you can work with. If the $30 floor breaks, you just stay away.
questions.lesson_line: Let the breakout pick the direction. The textbook lean doesn't.

wrong.Short now, the pattern is bearish: That's trading the label, and these break up about as often as down. We only recommend shorting to traders who have already made $1 million trading.
wrong.Buy now, the floor will hold: Floors break too. Nothing's confirmed yet.
wrong.Wait for a bounce off $30, then buy: A bounce off the floor isn't a breakout. It's still a guess inside the pattern.

questions.simple: Wait for price to break one of the lines. These break either way, whatever the label says.

deeper.trap: The textbook label and the data disagree here. StockCharts calls the descending triangle bearish, yet Bulkowski counts upward breakouts 53% of the time. The close outside a line removes the guess: it shows which way price actually went.
deeper.example: Fidelity's guide says descending triangles break most commonly downward. Bulkowski confirms the pattern only on a close outside a line.

reasons: a statistic that changes as Bulkowski updates his tables (53% upward)

questions.story: A stock has traded between $20 and $25 for months. One day it drops to $19.40, then closes back at $20.60.
questions.q: What's that move called?
choices: Spring
Breakdown
Upthrust
Throwback
questions.why: A spring. It dipped under the $20 floor to $19.40, then closed back inside at $20.60. Everyone with a stop just under $20 got shaken out, and the stock took it right back. That undercut and reclaim of support is a move I like in a good stock. The close back inside the range is the tell, so wait for it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring dips under support and closes back inside the range.

wrong.Breakdown: It did dip under $20, but it closed back inside at $20.60. That close makes it a spring.
wrong.Upthrust: An upthrust happens at the top of the range. This dipped under the floor.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback is a dip back to the breakout price after an upside break. This stock never broke out.

questions.simple: A spring. Price broke under the $20 floor, then closed back inside the range.

deeper.trap: Not every dip under support is a spring. The test is the close: back inside the range, as here at $20.60. Wait for the close before you name it.
deeper.example: The StockCharts glossary calls a break below support that soon reverses back above it a spring. The Wyckoff tutorial and the CMT Association say the same.

questions.q: Your buddy texts that his stock 'just had a shakeout.' What happened?
choices: A sharp dip that scares holders out
A slow, steady slide over many months
A gap up on strong earnings news
A week of very tiny daily ranges
questions.answer: A sharp dip that scares holders out
questions.why: A sharp dip that scared holders out. Bad news or plain nerves, and a lot of people sell at once, often at a loss. It's fast, a drop off recent highs. In a strong stock I like these. A shakeout under a key level that recovers fast can be a great spot to get involved. Keep the stop tight, under the low.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout runs scared holders out, and it's fast.

wrong.A gap up on strong earnings news: That rewards holders. A shakeout scares them out.
wrong.A week of very tiny daily ranges: That's a quiet, tight stock. A shakeout is a sharp drop.
wrong.A slow, steady slide over many months: That's a slow bleed. A shakeout is a fast drop where many sell at once.

questions.simple: A sharp drop that scared a lot of holders into selling at once, often at a loss.

deeper.example: The StockCharts glossary: many scared investors exit their positions on bad news or uncertainty. Investopedia: many investors exit at the same time, often at a loss, and shakeouts are usually sharp drops from recent highs.

questions.q: A stock spends months in a range before a big run. In Wyckoff's terms, what's the cause?
choices: The range's build-up behind a move
The news that started the big selloff
The breakout day's volume spike
The trend before the range began
questions.answer: The range's build-up behind a move
questions.why: The build-up inside the range. Wyckoff called it cause and effect. The buying or selling that piles up inside the range is the cause. The move out of the range is the effect. A bigger build-up means a bigger cause behind the move. It's the old way of saying the base sets up the run.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff: the range builds the cause, and the trend that follows is the effect.

wrong.The news that started the big selloff: News can start a move, but Wyckoff's cause is built inside the range.
wrong.The breakout day's volume spike: That's the move leaving the range, the start of the effect.
wrong.The trend before the range began: That came before the range. The cause is built inside it.

questions.simple: The build-up inside the range. The move that comes out of the range is the effect.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f198)

deeper.example: In Wyckoff's law of cause and effect, the accumulation or distribution inside a trading range is the cause. The move out of it is the effect. Wyckoff Analytics measures the cause with a point count on a Point-and-Figure chart. Pruden's CMT slides describe the same idea.

questions.q: Your stock's range never undercut its floor. By Wyckoff's method, that range can't be accumulation.
questions.why: False. A spring is optional. One of Wyckoff's two accumulation sketches has a spring, and the other has none at all. Plenty of good bases build without ever undercutting the floor. When you do get a spring, take it as a bonus.
questions.lesson_line: No spring doesn't mean no base. It's optional.
questions.simple: False, a spring is optional. One of the two Wyckoff sketches shows a range with no spring.

deeper.counter: Schematic 1 shows a spring, so it's easy to treat one as required. Schematic 2 shows a trading range with no spring at all. The Wyckoff tutorial calls springs and terminal shakeouts not required elements.

reasons: one shared text: StockCharts republishes the Wyckoff Analytics tutorial

questions.q: You hear 'flat base' on a leader you're tracking. What's the stock doing?
choices: Sideways for several weeks or more
A steep, sudden run on volume
A V-shaped drop, then recovery
A gap left unfilled for weeks
questions.answer: Sideways for several weeks or more
questions.why: Going sideways for several weeks or more. Price keeps tagging about the same high and the same low, like a rectangle. It's a pause, not a direction. We buy flat bases in leaders as price trades through the top of the base. The breakout decides what comes next.
questions.lesson_line: Flat base: the stock moves sideways, neither up nor down, for weeks.

wrong.A steep, sudden run on volume: That's a flagpole, a quick run. A flat base goes sideways.
wrong.A V-shaped drop, then recovery: A V is a sharp reversal. A flat base goes sideways.
wrong.A gap left unfilled for weeks: That's a price gap, not weeks of sideways trading.

questions.simple: Moving sideways for weeks or months, not rising or falling much.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10); IBD shows only its opening, Bulkowski confirmed

deeper.example: Bulkowski says a flat base looks like a rectangle: price touches the same value multiple times over several weeks or months. IBD says the stock moves sideways rather than going on an uptrend or downtrend.

questions.q: An old-school trader says his stock is 'in a Darvas box.' What's he describing?
choices: A range set by recent highs and lows
A rounded base with a short handle
A flat top with rising lows
Three peaks, middle highest
questions.answer: A range set by recent highs and lows
questions.why: A range set by recent highs and lows. Darvas drew a box around the stock: a top it couldn't clear and a bottom it held. He bought the break above the box on strong volume. It's not a shape like a cup or a triangle. It's just the range the stock is in, and the trade comes on the break.
questions.lesson_line: Darvas box: a top, a bottom, and a trade on the break.
questions.simple: A price range framed by recent highs and lows. The trade comes on a break above it.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10); Investopedia unreachable for this check, Bulkowski confirmed

deeper.example: Investopedia says the Darvas box places price in a box based on recent highs and lows. The buy signal is a break above the box on strong volume. Bulkowski sets the box top at a high that holds for the next three days. Then he waits for a close outside the box.

questions.q: Your flag's measured target is $38. That number tells you how far price will go.
questions.why: False. A measured target is a rough guide. It's arithmetic on the pattern's height, not a forecast. Price can stall short of $38 or run way past it. I sell into strength on a push and trail the rest. I don't sit and wait for a printed number.
questions.lesson_line: A measured target is a rough guide, not a forecast.
questions.simple: False, a measured target is only a rough guess. Price can stop short of it or run past it.

deeper.trap: A target printed on the chart looks precise, down to the cent. That precision comes from arithmetic, not from a forecast. Bulkowski says the computation varies from pattern to pattern and is usually inaccurate.
deeper.example: StockCharts says any price target should serve as a rough guide, and other factors should also be considered. Bulkowski calls the result an estimate only.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Your cup with handle just broke out clean. From here, it rarely gives much back.
questions.why: False. Plenty of them give a lot back. In a study of 300 cups, 47% dropped substantially within two months of the breakout. A throwback to the breakout price is common too. So a clean breakout is a start, not a safe spot. Your stop goes in the moment you buy.
questions.lesson_line: A clean breakout still needs a stop. Nearly half gave back a lot.
questions.simple: False, many cup breakouts give back a lot. In one study 47% dropped hard within two months.

deeper.trap: A clean breakout feels like proof. Bulkowski's numbers say otherwise: 47% of the 300 cups he studied dropped substantially within two months. Plan the stop before the breakout, not after the drop.
deeper.example: Fidelity's guide says cups with handles often have a throwback, a return to the breakout price. Bulkowski studied 300 of them from 1990 to March 2024.

reasons: a study statistic that changes as Bulkowski updates it (47%, 300 patterns)
fixed before (checker added f197 and f182)

questions.story: You buy a cup with handle breakout at $50.10. The handle dipped to $47 before the breakout.
questions.q: Where does the textbook put your stop?
choices: Just under the handle's low
No stop until the target hits
Lower it if price gets close
Right at the $50.10 buy price
questions.why: Just under the handle's low, near $47. Bulkowski names the handle low as a good place for a stop. Investopedia puts stops below the handle or the cup, by risk tolerance. Set it before you buy. Then raise it as price rises, as Bulkowski advises.
questions.lesson_line: Set the stop before you buy. The handle's low is the natural line.

wrong.No stop until the target hits: Hope isn't a stop. Bulkowski found 47% of these dropped substantially within two months of the breakout.
wrong.Lower it if price gets close: That widens the loss you planned for. Bulkowski's advice runs the other way: raise the stop as price rises.
wrong.Right at the $50.10 buy price: That leaves no room. Fidelity's guide says cups with handles often have a throwback, a return to the breakout price.

questions.simple: The textbook stop goes just under the handle's low near $47, a level Bulkowski names as a good stop.

deeper.trap: Two mistakes sit on either side of the right stop. With no stop, nothing caps the loss: Bulkowski found 47% of these dropped substantially within two months. A stop right at the buy is so tight that a normal throwback to the breakout price can set it off.

reasons: touches the owner's stop rules (A3, F62, A13): the textbook stop is wider
fixed before (handle low and a wrong-note changed)

questions.q: Three peaks after a long slide aren't a head and shoulders top. A top needs an uptrend in front of it.
questions.why: True. A top is a turn down, so there has to be an uptrend to turn. No run-up, nothing to reverse. A small rise into it means a small drop out of it, if any. People new to charts see head and shoulders everywhere. Check the trend leading in before you name it.
questions.lesson_line: No uptrend before it, no head and shoulders top.
questions.simple: True, a top is a turn down. Without an uptrend before it, there's nothing to turn.

deeper.counter: Picture three peaks with the middle one highest, drawn after a long slide. The outline matches, but there's no uptrend to reverse, so StockCharts wouldn't call it a head and shoulders top. Schwab warns that people new to technical analysis tend to see these patterns everywhere.
deeper.example: StockCharts says that without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a head and shoulders reversal. Bulkowski adds that a small rise into the pattern means a small expected decline.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.story: After a long slide, a stock makes three lows: $30, then $26, then $30.50. The rally highs between them sit near $34.
questions.q: What's forming here?
choices: Inverse head and shoulders
Triple bottom near $30
Rounding bottom, or saucer
Head and shoulders top
questions.why: An inverse head and shoulders. The middle low at $26 is the deepest, and that's the head. The lows at $30 and $30.50 on each side are the shoulders. A triple bottom would need all three near the same price, and $26 sits way under the others. The rally highs near $34 are the neckline, the level to watch.
questions.lesson_line: Deep middle low, level lows either side: the bottom version of head and shoulders.

wrong.Head and shoulders top: A top is built from peaks, not lows.
wrong.Triple bottom near $30: A triple bottom's three lows sit at about the same price. The $26 low is far below the others.
wrong.Rounding bottom, or saucer: A saucer is one slow, rounded low. Here there are three separate lows.

questions.simple: An inverse head and shoulders. The $26 low in the middle is deepest, and the outer lows sit near $30.

deeper.trap: A long slide and three lows close together invite the triple bottom label. Look at the depth of the middle low. Here the middle one, $26, sits well under the $30 and $30.50 lows on either side. So it's the head, not a third equal low.
deeper.example: StockCharts calls this three troughs with the middle one deepest, and Bulkowski a 3-valley pattern with the middle valley below the others.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: You're hunting for a rounding bottom that took most of a year to form. Which chart do you pull up?
choices: A weekly chart
An intraday chart
A one-month daily chart
A long daily chart
questions.why: A weekly chart. A rounding bottom takes many months, and that slow curve is hard to see on a daily. Zoom out and the bowl shows up. A one-month daily cuts it off completely. Make it a habit to check the weekly on everything you trade.
questions.lesson_line: Slow patterns need a zoomed-out chart. Check the weekly.

wrong.An intraday chart: Way too short. This pattern takes many months.
wrong.A one-month daily chart: A month barely covers a piece of the bowl.
wrong.A long daily chart: More days help, but the slow curve is still hard to spot there. The weekly shows it.

questions.simple: A weekly chart. The bowl takes many months, and its slow curve is easiest to see there.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts calls the rounding bottom a long-term reversal pattern best suited for weekly charts. Bulkowski says rounding bottoms are difficult to spot unless you look on the weekly scale.

questions.q: A shakeout in a strong stock is a scare inside the uptrend, not the end of it.
questions.why: True. A shakeout happens inside a longer uptrend, and after it the trend often picks back up. Often, not always. If the drop takes out your stop, you're out, no debate. You can buy it back when it sets up again.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is a scare, not a verdict. Often the prior trend picks back up.
questions.simple: True, a shakeout is a scare inside an uptrend, and the trend often comes back after it.

deeper.trap: Calling a drop a shakeout is no promise. Investopedia says the prior trend often reasserts, not that it must. The Wyckoff tutorial says shakeouts aim to make holders sell to large operators.
deeper.example: Investopedia uses shakeout almost only for an interruption in a longer-term bullish trend.

reasons: fixed before (statement rewritten by the checker)

questions.story: A stock breaks out of an ascending triangle at $40. It rises to $41.50, stalls, then closes below the triangle's low at $36.
questions.q: What do you call this?
choices: A busted pattern
A routine throwback
A Wyckoff spring
A bullish shakeout
questions.why: A busted pattern. It broke out at $40 and only got to $41.50. Then it closed below the triangle's low at $36. The breakout failed and price went out the other side. If you bought the break, your stop had you out long before that. Respect it. A busted pattern can start a move the other way.
questions.lesson_line: When a breakout fails and price exits the other side, respect it.

wrong.A routine throwback: A throwback dips back to the breakout price. This fell through the whole pattern.
wrong.A Wyckoff spring: A spring dips under support and closes back inside. This closed below the whole triangle.
wrong.A bullish shakeout: A shakeout comes back. This closed under the triangle's low and stayed there.

questions.simple: A busted pattern. Price barely rose after the break, then closed below the whole triangle.

deeper.trap: Calling it a shakeout and waiting for a bounce is the trap. The close below the triangle's low says the breakout failed.
deeper.example: Bulkowski's busted pattern: price rises less than 10% after the breakout, reverses, and closes below the bottom of the pattern. He adds that a busted pattern can start a trend in the new direction. Fidelity's guide calls it a failed breakout, or trap.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f183)

questions.story: You bought a flag breakout. Its measured target is $38. Price stalls at $36, then the whole market sells off hard.
questions.q: Do you hold on for the $38 target?
choices: No, reassess: conditions changed
Yes, the target is the plan
Yes, and add to get there faster
No, widen the stop to give it room
questions.why: No, reassess. The $38 was an estimate you made before the market rolled over. Conditions changed, so the plan gets a second look. Keep your stop where it is, or sell some. Adding or widening the stop does the opposite of what you want. Trade what's in front of you, not a number you drew last week.
questions.lesson_line: The target was an estimate made earlier. Trade what's in front of you now.

wrong.Yes, the target is the plan: A target is an estimate, not a promise from the market.
wrong.Yes, and add to get there faster: Adding into a selloff to chase a target doubles down on a guess.
wrong.No, widen the stop to give it room: That raises the loss you planned for. Stops move up as price rises, never down.

questions.simple: No. The target was only an estimate, and the market has changed since you set it.

deeper.trap: A target set before a market selloff is a guess about a market that has since changed. Fidelity's guide calls holding to it a dangerous habit.
deeper.example: Fidelity's pattern guide lists sticking with a pattern's original target after conditions change among the dangerous habits. Bulkowski calls any target an estimate only, and says to raise the stop as price rises.

reasons: fixed before (question reworded by the checker)

questions.story: A stock forms what looks like an inverse head and shoulders. It's at $33, just under its $34 neckline. A friend wants to buy now to get in early.
questions.q: What do you tell him?
choices: Wait for it to break $34
Buy now, the shape is done
Buy half now, half at $34
Wait for a retest of the head's low
questions.why: Wait for it to break $34. At $33 it's still just a shape. The neckline is the trigger. We buy as price trades through $34 during the day, with the stop under the low of the day. The textbooks wait for a close above it, same idea, a little later. A slightly better fill at $33 is no help if the neckline holds and it rolls over.
questions.lesson_line: Early is a guess. The neckline break is the signal.

wrong.Buy now, the shape is done: A shape isn't a pattern until it breaks out. At $33 it hasn't.
wrong.Buy half now, half at $34: Half bought on a guess is still a guess. Nothing's confirmed under $34.
wrong.Wait for a retest of the head's low: A drop back to the head's low would wreck the shape. The signal is the break of $34.

questions.simple: Wait for $34 to break. The pattern isn't confirmed until price clears the neckline.

deeper.trap: Buying at $33 feels like a better price than the breakout. The cost is that the shape may never confirm. Schwab says many investors have paid a steep price for placing a trade without waiting for signals confirming the pattern.
deeper.example: Bulkowski says to wait for confirmation before placing a trade, and confirms this pattern on a close above the neckline. StockCharts wants the neckline break to come convincingly, with an expansion of volume.

reasons: keyed as the textbook view; UCT's own entry timing on a neckline break (close or intraday) is not in the rulebook

questions.q: Ascending triangles break down too, not just up.
questions.why: True. In one big count of these, about 63% broke up, so the rest broke down. The flat top and rising lows give it a bullish lean, and that's all a lean is. Set the alert at the flat top and buy as price trades through it. If it breaks down instead, you never bought it, and it cost you nothing.
questions.lesson_line: Bullish lean, not a guarantee. Plan for the break you don't expect.
questions.simple: True, about 63% broke up in one big count, so the rest broke down.

deeper.trap: The flat top and rising lows look like buyers winning, so it's easy to buy early, hoping for the upside break. Bulkowski's own count still has a share of these breaking down.
deeper.example: Bulkowski counts upward breakouts 63% of the time. Fidelity's guide says prices can break either way, but more commonly upward. StockCharts gives the pattern a bullish bias from its rising lows.

reasons: rests on a study count (Bulkowski's 63%) that he updates over time

questions.q: Wedges rank among the best-performing chart patterns you can trade.
questions.why: False. They test poorly. In one big pattern study, rising wedges rank among the worst performers, and falling wedges do poorly among the bullish patterns. Pullbacks after the break are very common too. The lean tells you which way it lands more often, not that it pays. I'd rather spend my time on flags and bases in leaders.
questions.lesson_line: Wedges test poorly. Know the shape, but don't build your trading around it.
questions.simple: False, tests put rising wedges among the worst patterns, and falling wedges do poorly too.

deeper.counter: Textbooks give the falling wedge a bullish bias and the rising wedge a bearish one, which can sound like a strong edge. The bias only tells you which way the break leans. On Bulkowski's and Fidelity's reading both wedges rate below average.
deeper.example: Bulkowski says rising wedges, especially with downward breakouts, are some of the worst performing chart patterns. He calls the falling wedge a poor performer. Fidelity's guide says performance in both types is below average, and retracements are very common.

reasons: performance rankings come from study data that is updated over time

questions.q: Two charts show the same small triangle. Only one came right after a sharp run. What makes a pennant a pennant?
choices: Pennants are short, after sharp runs
Pennants have two parallel lines
Triangles need a long downtrend first
Pennants come with no flagpole
questions.answer: Pennants are short, after sharp runs
questions.why: Pennants are short and come after sharp runs. The lines close in the same way on both, so the shape won't tell you. The setting will. No pole, no pennant, however small it looks. And a pennant that drags on past about three weeks has turned into a symmetrical triangle. Check the pole first, then the clock.
questions.lesson_line: Same shape, different setting: a pennant hangs off a pole.

wrong.Pennants have two parallel lines: Parallel lines make a flag. A pennant's lines close in, like a triangle's.
wrong.Triangles need a long downtrend first: The trend into a symmetrical triangle can go either way.
wrong.Pennants come with no flagpole: It's the reverse. A pennant needs a sharp move, its pole, before it.

questions.simple: A pennant is short and comes right after a sharp run. A triangle can form without one.

deeper.trap: A small triangle with no sharp run before it isn't a pennant, however short. A pennant that runs past three weeks becomes a symmetrical triangle in Bulkowski's book.
deeper.example: Investopedia: flags and pennants need a sudden shift before they form, and symmetrical triangles can form without one. StockCharts calls a symmetrical triangle under three weeks a pennant.

reasons: fixed before (checker removed absolute words from two wrong choices)

questions.q: A stock fails three times near the same high. The lows between are level, then they break. Name it.
choices: Triple top
Head and shoulders
Double top
Ascending triangle
questions.why: A triple top. Three tries at the same high, three failures, then the floor gives way. The level lows rule out an ascending triangle, where the lows rise. In a head and shoulders the middle peak stands taller. It's done only when the lows break. If you're long, your stop should have you out by then.
questions.lesson_line: Triple top: three equal highs, done only when support breaks.

wrong.Head and shoulders: Its middle peak stands taller than the other two. Here all three are level.
wrong.Double top: That's only two peaks. This one failed three times.
wrong.Ascending triangle: Its lows rise toward a flat top. Here the lows are level.

questions.simple: A triple top. Three tries at the same high fail, then the lows between them break.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: StockCharts describes three equal highs followed by a break below support. Fidelity's guide describes three peaks at about the same price with two troughs between.

questions.q: Your stock pops above the top of its range in the morning, then closes back inside it. What's that called?
choices: Upthrust
Spring
Breakout
Throwback
questions.why: An upthrust. A push above resistance that fails fast and closes back in the range. It's the mirror of a spring. If you bought that pop as it traded through the top, you're now in a failed breakout. Your stop a few cents under the low of the day is what keeps that loss small.
questions.lesson_line: Upthrust: a push above the range that closes back inside it.

wrong.Spring: A spring dips below the range's floor, not above its top.
wrong.Breakout: A breakout holds outside the range. This one closed back inside.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback is a dip back to the breakout price after a breakout that held. This one never held.

questions.simple: An upthrust. Price pushes above the range's top, then quickly closes back inside it.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

deeper.example: The Wyckoff tutorial calls an upthrust a price move above trading range resistance that quickly reverses and closes inside the range. The CMT Association describes the same sharp thrust above resistance and quick close back below it.

questions.story: You buy a cup with handle breakout at $50.10. Today's low so far is $49.60. The handle bottomed at $47.
questions.q: Where's your stop?
choices: A few cents under today's $49.60 low
Exactly on today's $49.60 low
A few cents under the $47 handle low
Exactly on the $47 handle low
questions.answer: A few cents under today's $49.60 low
questions.why: A few cents under $49.60, the low of the day, or LOD. Not right on it, because a stop sitting on the exact low gets tagged by noise. From your $50.10 fill that's about 1%, a nice tight stop. The $47 handle low is the textbook stop, and it's acceptable on some setups. Here it's more than 5% away, wider than we'll take.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the low of the day, never right on it.
questions.simple: A few cents under today's $49.60 low. Not on it, and not down at the $47 handle low.

wrong.Exactly on today's $49.60 low: Right level, wrong spot. A stop right on the low gets clipped by noise. Put it a few cents under.
wrong.A few cents under the $47 handle low: That's the textbook stop. From your $50.10 fill it's more than 5% away, wider than we'll take.
wrong.Exactly on the $47 handle low: Too wide from $50.10, past 5%. And a stop right on a low gets clipped by noise.

deeper.example: Bulkowski calls the handle low a good place for a stop. Investopedia says the stop can go below the handle or below the cup. We start from the low of the day: 1-3% is where we like a stop, and up to 5% is acceptable.

conflicts: Double bottom lows: StockCharts accepts a second low within 3% of the first, Investopedia within 3% to 4%, Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slides 'roughly the same price'. IBD's double bottom (O'Neil) wants the second low to UNDERCUT the first, and Bulkowski's 'ugly double bottom' has the second low 5% to 15% HIGHER. q40 asks only the computed gap and StockCharts' 3% reading of 'roughly equal'; no question says the second low must undercut or must sit higher. IBD's undercut rule could not be quoted: investors.com shows this client only each article's first paragraph.

Descending triangle direction: StockCharts calls it bearish and Fidelity's guide says it breaks 'most commonly downward'; Bulkowski's current table says upward 53% of the time. No question keys a direction; q44 keys the point all three allow (wait for the close outside a line) and names both readings in the reveal.

Flag and pennant length: StockCharts' flag article says one to 12 weeks (ideally one to four), its glossary says flags 'generally' last under three weeks, Bulkowski says under three weeks, Investopedia's pennant page one to three weeks. No question keys a length. q31 uses a four-month flag, past both StockCharts' 12 weeks and Bulkowski's three, so both call it a rectangle (checker: it said 'for months', and StockCharts still calls a two-month flag a flag).
Cup length: Bulkowski and Investopedia give 7 to 65 weeks; StockCharts and Fidelity's indicator guide say one to six months. Not asked.

Cup with handle entry: IBD uses the handle's highest price plus 10 cents; Investopedia a buy stop slightly above the handle's upper trend line (or a close above it); Fidelity's guide a break through the cup's right side; Bulkowski a close above the right cup rim, or an earlier close above a down-sloping handle trendline. q27 keys the shared part, 'just above the top of the handle'.

Cup with handle stop: Bulkowski names the handle low; Investopedia allows below the handle or below the cup; Bulkowski's throwback study prefers two cents under the breakout day's low followed by a volatility stop. q53 keys the handle low (both Bulkowski and Investopedia allow it) and offers no other legitimate stop as a wrong choice.

Spring volume: the Wyckoff tutorial (StockCharts / Wyckoff Analytics) reads a LOW-volume spring as a sign the stock is ready to rise; the CMT Association's 'Reversal Bars' piece says volume on a spring is 'typically quite high (the higher the better)'. No question mentions volume on a spring; q45's story gives none.

Spring sources: the StockCharts ChartSchool Wyckoff tutorial and the Wyckoff Analytics page carry the same text (StockCharts republishes it). The spring definition questions also rest on independently worded definitions: StockCharts' glossary entry and the CMT Association piece. The cause question (q47) now also cites independently written slides by Hank Pruden hosted by the CMT Association (s57, checker). q48 (springs are optional) still rests on the shared tutorial text alone (StockCharts plus Wyckoff Analytics, the method's own school); the checker's search found no other reliable source, only vendor blogs.

Saucer: StockCharts (article and glossary) and Bulkowski ('saucer lip') use saucer for the rounding bottom. Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slide titles the cup and handle 'Cup and Handle (also Saucer)'. q20 keys the StockCharts/Bulkowski usage.
Rounding bottom: StockCharts treats it as a reversal after a decline; Bulkowski finds price trending UP into it 67% of the time (acting as a continuation). Not asked.

Head and shoulders target: StockCharts, Fidelity and Schwab project the full head-to-neckline height; Bulkowski multiplies it by his 'percentage meeting price target' (51% for tops). q43 asks the textbook full-height method and calls it a rough guide.

Wedge touches: StockCharts asks for at least two reaction highs (ideally three) and two reaction lows; Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide want at least five touches (three on one line, two on the other). q33 names Bulkowski and Fidelity.

Pullback: Bulkowski and Fidelity's slides use 'pullback' for a return to the breakout price after a DOWNWARD breakout; V.02 teaches the everyday meaning (a dip in an uptrend). This unit does not ask the pattern-book meaning.

Shakeout: StockCharts' glossary and Investopedia define it broadly (many investors exit at once); the Wyckoff tutorial describes shakeouts engineered by large operators. Investopedia says the word is used almost only for an interruption in a longer uptrend, but the Wyckoff tutorial says shakeouts 'may also' come once an advance has started and StockCharts' glossary example is the dot-com bust, a decline. So no question says shakeouts usually come in uptrends: q46 keys the broad meaning; q57 (rewritten by the checker) keys only that a shakeout does not by itself mean the uptrend is over (Investopedia: the prior trend often reasserts; Wyckoff: shakeouts inside an advance).
